# inlavanilla <img src="man/figures/logo.png" align="right" height="139" alt="inlavanilla hex logo" />

<!-- badges: start -->

[![R-CMD-check](https://github.com/haziqj/inlavanilla/actions/workflows/R-CMD-check.yaml/badge.svg)](https://github.com/haziqj/inlavanilla/actions/workflows/R-CMD-check.yaml)
[![Codecov test coverage](https://codecov.io/gh/haziqj/inlavanilla/graph/badge.svg)](https://app.codecov.io/gh/haziqj/inlavanilla)

<!-- badges: end -->

> INLA-style skew-normal marginals for any log-posterior.

If you can write down the log-likelihood plus the log-prior, `{inlavanilla}`
gives you approximate Bayesian inference for the parameters of your model:
posterior marginals and draws, the marginal likelihood, and leave-one-out
cross-validation. There is no sampler and no tuning, and small models take
milliseconds. It runs the
approximation pipeline of [INLAvaan](https://inlavaan.haziqj.ml/) with
nothing model-specific:

1. a **Laplace approximation** at the posterior mode, with the Laplace
   estimate of the log marginal likelihood;
2. a **VB mean correction** that recentres the Gaussian at a better estimate
   of the posterior mean;
3. **skew-normal marginals**, one per parameter, fitted to scans of the
   log-posterior;
4. **Gaussian copula draws** for any function of the parameters.

Stages 2 and 3 are optional and independent: `vb = FALSE` skips the VB
correction, and `marginals = "gaussian"` keeps the Gaussian marginals instead
of scanning for skew-normal ones. With both, you get the Laplace approximation
alone.

Give `loo()` or `waic()` the log-likelihood as one term per observation, and
they estimate the model's predictive accuracy from the fit alone, with no
refits and no draws.

The package is pure R and small. Its only dependency outside base R is
[cli](https://cli.r-lib.org/).

## Installation

You can install the development version of inlavanilla from
[GitHub](https://github.com/haziqj/inlavanilla) with:

``` r
# install.packages("pak")
pak::pak("haziqj/inlavanilla")
```

## Example

A trial records 3 responders out of 20 patients. With a uniform prior on the
response rate $p$, the posterior is $\text{Beta}(4, 18)$: skewed, and bounded
at zero.

`inla_vanilla()` works on an unconstrained scale, so we write the
log-posterior in terms of $\vartheta = \text{logit}(p)$. The prior is
stated for $p$, so it carries the Jacobian $dp / d\vartheta = p(1 - p)$:

```{r example}
library(inlavanilla)

logpost <- function(theta, y, n) {
  p <- plogis(theta[["logit_p"]])
  dbinom(y, n, p, log = TRUE) +
    dbeta(p, 1, 1, log = TRUE) + # prior on p ...
    log(p) + log1p(-p) # ... and the Jacobian
}

fit <- inla_vanilla(logpost, init = c(logit_p = 0), y = 3, n = 20)
fit
```

The summary is on the logit scale. `sampling()` draws from the approximate
posterior, and its `fun` argument maps each draw back to $p$, or to any other
quantity of interest:

```{r draws}
set.seed(1)
p <- sampling(
  fit,
  nsamp = 1e5,
  fun = function(theta) plogis(theta[["logit_p"]])
)
rbind(
  inlavanilla = quantile(p, c(0.025, 0.5, 0.975)),
  exact = qbeta(c(0.025, 0.5, 0.975), 4, 18)
)
```

The approximation matches the exact posterior, skew included:

```{r density, fig.height = 3.5, fig.alt = "Histogram of draws of p, skewed to the right, with the exact Beta(4, 18) density overlaid and matching it."}
hist(p, breaks = 80, freq = FALSE, border = NA, col = "#F5D0BE",
     main = NULL, xlab = "Response rate p", ylab = NULL, yaxt = "n")
curve(dbeta(x, 4, 18), add = TRUE, lwd = 2, col = "#C2410C")
```

`summary(fit)` adds diagnostics for each stage of the approximation, and
`plot(fit)` draws the marginals. The
[Get started](http://haziqj.ml/inlavanilla/articles/inlavanilla.html)
vignette works through a multi-parameter example: it checks the approximation
against the exact posterior, and covers gradients, derived quantities and
model comparison.
